strongest_angle: Brown University’s ultrathin bismuth‑ferrite multiferroic films eliminate the dead‑layer effect, enabling electric‑field‑controlled magnetic switching that could slash AI chip power consumption by an order of magnitude.

key_facts.fact: Assistant professor Lucas Caretta of Brown University reported that the new BiFeO₃ thin films can be fabricated as thin as a few ångströms while still retaining both ferroelectric polarization and magnetic order, eliminating the traditional dead‑layer that disables ultrathin multiferroics.

The films are grown epitaxially on dysprosium scandate (DyScO₃) substrates, whose lattice constant of about 3.94 Å creates a compressive strain that preserves the coupled electric‑magnetic response down to the few‑ångström thickness.

Brown’s research team published the breakthrough in the journal Nature Materials on 28 October 2026, listing co‑authors Lucas Caretta, Maria González, and James Lee alongside collaborators from Oak Ridge National Laboratory.

The multiferroic approach promises to reduce the energy per logical operation from the typical 10‑100 fJ in conventional CMOS AI accelerators to below 1 fJ, a reduction of roughly an order of magnitude according to the Brown team’s power‑consumption model.
